batchName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE)

questions.question: Which institutions did the rebel state of Italia have? (select all that apply)
options: Twelve generals
A senate of 500 members
A single dictator
Two consuls
A king elected for life
A senate of 300 members
questions.explanation: The rebels’ state, Italia, had a senate of 500 members, two consuls and twelve generals, with its capital at Corfinium.
questions.sourceQuote: It had a forum, a senate of 500 members, two consuls and twelve generals.

questions.question: When and under whom did Sulla's military career begin?
options: In 138 BC under his noble father
In 91 BC under the tribune Drusus
In 90 BC at the Tolenus River
In 101 BC against Germanic invaders
In 133 BC under the land reformers
In 107 BC under Marius in Numidia
questions.explanation: Sulla started as a junior officer under Marius, who was fighting a rebellious king in Numidia. He later served again in the wars against Germanic invaders.
questions.sourceQuote: His career began in 107 BC as a junior officer under Marius, then fighting a rebellious king in Numidia, a kingdom in North Africa.

questions.question: By 218 BC, what was the ratio of allied soldiers to Roman soldiers in Rome's armies?
options: Two allies for every Roman
Three allies for every two Romans
One ally for every three Romans
One ally for every Roman
Two allies for every three Romans
Four allies for every Roman
questions.explanation: Allies made up the majority of Rome's armies, which made them indispensable. They shared in the plunder in return.
questions.sourceQuote: By 218 BC, Rome's armies held three allied soldiers for every two Romans.

questions.question: Which of these happened during or after Sulla's first march on Rome in 88 BC? (select all that apply)
options: Citizens threw stones from the rooftops
The Senate greeted him with a triumph
Marius fled to Greece to join Mithridates
Marius and eleven others were declared public enemies
His soldiers mutinied and killed him
His officers deserted him
questions.explanation: Sulla faced deserting officers and hostile citizens but still took Rome and outlawed Marius and eleven others. Marius fled to Africa, not Greece.
questions.sourceQuote: His officers deserted him, and citizens hurled stones from the rooftops.

questions.question: Which statement about the Battle of the Colline Gate in 82 BC is accurate?
options: Marius commanded the army opposing Sulla
Sulla's own wing broke, but his right wing won
It was fought the day Sulla landed in Italy
Sulla's wing won while his right wing collapsed
It was fought against an army of Mithridates
Sulla pardoned all his prisoners the next day
questions.explanation: Sulla's own wing gave way, but his right wing secured victory. The next day, thousands of prisoners were butchered within earshot of the Senate as he addressed it.
questions.sourceQuote: Sulla's own wing broke, but his right wing won.

questions.question: What surviving evidence comes from the Italian side of the Social War?
options: Treaty texts written in Oscan
A Samnite chronicle of the war
Letters from Italia's two consuls
Only a few coins
Inscriptions listing Italia's senators
The memoirs of the Marsic commander
questions.explanation: No Italian narrative survives, only a few coins. That gap is one reason historians still argue about what the rebels wanted.
questions.sourceQuote: No Italian account survives, apart from a few coins.

questions.question: Which town, the rebels' new capital, did Sulla capture in 89 BC?
options: Asculum
Corfinium
Bovianum
Pompeii
Puteoli
Nola
questions.explanation: After taking Pompeii and winning the grass crown near Nola, Sulla captured Bovianum. The same year, Asculum fell after a long siege.
questions.sourceQuote: He then captured the rebels' new capital at Bovianum.

questions.question: When was the registration of the newly enfranchised Italians finally completed?
options: During Sulla's dictatorship
Immediately after the fall of Asculum
In 88 BC, before the march on Rome
It was abandoned and never completed
Within a year of the Julian Law
Only under Rome's first emperor
questions.explanation: Registration dragged on for decades. Meanwhile Italy was scarred, with the central mountains devastated.
questions.sourceQuote: Registration dragged on for decades and was completed only under Rome's first emperor.

questions.question: How did the last band of Samnite and Lucanian holdouts finally obtain Roman citizenship?
options: By bargaining with one faction during Rome's own civil strife
Through a revived version of Drusus's laws
By surrendering under the terms of the Julian Law
By a special grant from Sulla as dictator
By winning a decisive victory at the Colline Gate
By allying with Mithridates against Rome
questions.explanation: After the last organised rebel army was crushed in 88 BC, these holdouts fought on until 87 BC. Rome's internal conflict let them trade support for citizenship.
questions.sourceQuote: Then Rome's own civil strife let them win citizenship by bargaining with one faction.

questions.question: Which features applied to the dictatorship Sulla revived? (select all that apply)
options: It carried immunity for past and future acts
It was shared with a co-dictator
It had no time limit
The office had been unused for more than a century
It was limited to the traditional six months
It required re-election by the assembly each year
questions.explanation: Sulla revived a long-dormant office and gave it almost unlimited power, no time limit and full immunity. He nonetheless laid it down around the start of 80 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: This time the office came with no time limit and almost unlimited power.
